newsitem.title: GERMANY: Central banks need independence - SNB's Meyer.
newsitem.headline: Central banks need independence - SNB's Meyer.

text.p: Swiss National Bank president Hans Meyer stressed the importance of central bank independence, saying that this was needed to ensure price stability.

"It is in the nature of things that guaranteeing price stability belongs to the duties of a central bank, while other goals, such as for example fighting unemployment, remain in the background," Meyer said in the text of a speech to be presented at Humboldt University here.
He added that reducing unemployment was no less an important goal than price stability. But he said that monetary policy was not a proper means to reduce joblessness.
"Monetary policy is not a fitting instrument for this," Meyer said.
"I am of the opinion that the priority of price stability should be upheld in the constitution," he added.

Elsewhere in the speech he noted: "Price stability is the foremost goal of central banks. Short-term political influences can best be deflected by a central bank if it is legally mandated with respect to this priority."
Meyer noted a Swiss law, under article 89 of the draft Swiss constitution, explicitly outlines that the SNB is to maintain its independence.
"We greet this formulation," he said, adding that in the new Constitution the independent status was more clearly anchored than had been the case in the past.

Meyer said Swiss law spells out that the Swiss Federal Council and the Central Bank are required to notify each other of intentions and coordinate decisions which are considered likely to have significant impact on the economy or monetary policy.

Meyer also said the European Union in its new law governing the European Central Bank and respective member country central banks had adopted an even more strict policy, which forbids the European Central Bank and respective national banks from taking directions either from special groups, or from governments.

He said he had often stressed in the past "how problematic it is, when national deficits are financed by the central bank." Current Swiss law, he said, could also be made more explicit in this respect.
He said that it was necessary for the central bank to have public and political support for its goals.

"Parliaments and governments have a significant influence on the economic environment. If they conduct an unsound financial policy, even an independent central bank cannot create price stability. A central bank can only fullfil its role in a proper environment. Healthy federal finances are a large part of this," he said.

Meyer's speech was delivered only days after a conflict erupted between the German government and Bundesbank over Bonn's proposal to revalue German gold reserves. The move would help Germany reduce its federal budget deficit and so meet criteria to join the European single currency.
An SNB spokesman, in response to a query, acknowledged that Meyer's speech Friday in Berlin was "topical also due to the locality."
But, he said that when the subject was chosen for the talk, "it was not in view of the controversy at the moment."
